articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of those who support illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, and the implications of these designations, are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) released an update to its Iran designations on November 9, 2026.
This update signifies ongoing efforts to pressure the Iranian regime through economic sanctions.
The specific details of the updated designations are available on OFAC's official recent actions page.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Iran-related Designations
body: On November 6, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations.
These designations are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to counter Iran's destabilizing activities in the region and globally.
The full list of designated individuals and entities, along with the reasons for their designation, can be found on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Issues Cuba Designations and Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations.
Concurrently, OFAC issued new designations related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination, further tightening sanctions on the island nation.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating illicit activities across various fronts, from cybercrime to state-sponsored illicit finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran-related Designations, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL and FAQ
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to existing Iran-related listings.
In a comprehensive action, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question.
These measures reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy, adapting to evolving geopolitical landscapes and illicit finance threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
General Licenses provide specific authorizations for activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs.
The details of this amended license are crucial for entities engaged in permissible transactions involving Iran, and stakeholders are advised to review the updated guidance on the OFAC website.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting North Korea and individuals and entities related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
These actions aim to counter proliferation financing from North Korea and address human rights abuses and corruption in the DRC.
The designations underscore the U.S. commitment to using sanctions as a tool to promote international peace and security.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026.
The North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider agreed to pay $1,529,685 to resolve nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by designated entity JSC Concern Almaz Antey.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: On October 26, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These updates are part of OFAC's ongoing review process to ensure its published guidance remains current and clear for compliance professionals.
The revisions clarify existing requirements and procedures, particularly regarding reporting mechanisms and the distinction between blocking and rejecting transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses for Iran and Russia
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026.
In a separate action, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions policy in these areas.
Furthermore, OFAC issued new General Licenses for Iran and Russia, alongside amended Frequently Asked Questions, providing crucial guidance for permissible activities under these sanctions programs.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to a Russian defense manufacturer, JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA).

MMZA was deemed a blocked entity by operation of law due to its majority ownership by designated entity JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.
The violations, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism programs.
This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by FinCEN, the OCC, and OFAC, with total penalties exceeding $1.21 billion for AML and sanctions failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 for Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Regulations and the Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., a designated Chinese company involved in illicit drug trade.

OFAC found that Pegasus failed to adequately screen for the designated entity, which had changed its name but retained other SDN-listed identifiers, and also failed to fully respond to an OFAC subpoena for six months.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the individual's violations and the sanctions programs involved were not immediately disclosed in the public record.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on holding individuals accountable for sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a UAE-based distributor, knowing the goods were ultimately destined for an Iranian end-user.
These indirect sales took place between June 2019 and November 2021, after the revocation of General License H, which had previously authorized such transactions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles for $1,050,000 Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington, D.C.-based global advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle six apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.
Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List.

The violations stemmed from FTI's engagement, via a law firm, to provide expert economic consulting services in support of VTB, where delayed or partial payments effectively extended prohibited debt beyond the permissible 14-day maturity.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader, despite red flags indicating the LPG originated from Iran rather than Oman or Iraq.
AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar-denominated payments totaling approximately $192,104,044 for these shipments.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 for Multiple Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle 481 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs.

For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine, enabling them to execute securities-related transactions.
The violations stemmed from compliance control failures, including issues with geo-blocking software and a lack of oversight from sanctions compliance personnel.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the individual's violations and the sanctions programs involved were not immediately disclosed in the public record.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to pursuing sanctions breaches by individuals, including U.S. citizens residing abroad.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 for Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a Florida-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations.
Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements with two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

The school processed 89 related financial transactions, including wire transfers and credit card payments, for the benefit of the designees' children, despite their names matching entries on the SDN List.

articles.headline: Global Markets Show Mixed Performance Amidst Inflation Concerns
body: Global stock markets exhibited mixed performance this week as investors continued to grapple with persistent inflation concerns and the potential for further interest rate hikes by central banks.
Major indices in Asia saw slight gains, while European markets experienced minor declines. U.S. markets remained relatively flat, reflecting investor caution.
Analysts suggest that market volatility is likely to continue as economic data releases and central bank commentary shape expectations for future monetary policy.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Edge Upward on Supply Concerns and Geopolitical Tensions
body: Oil prices saw a modest increase this week, driven by ongoing concerns about global supply disruptions and escalating geopolitical tensions in key producing regions.
Brent crude futures rose by over 1%, while WTI crude also experienced a similar upward trend. The market remains sensitive to any developments that could impact crude oil availability.
Energy analysts are closely monitoring the situation, anticipating continued price fluctuations as supply-demand dynamics and international relations evolve.

articles.headline: ECB Signals Potential for Further Rate Hikes to Combat Inflation

This hawkish stance suggests that European consumers and businesses may face tighter borrowing conditions in the coming months.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
